summary: Discusses a proposed extension to the Internet architecture to provide integrated services, supporting real-time as well as non-real-time traffic. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet normally treats every packet the same and only tries its best to deliver it. This memo proposes a way to also promise some traffic, such as voice and video, a delivery time, and to share a busy link in a controlled way among groups. It describes the service model, the router mechanisms, and RSVP, the protocol that would set up the reservations.

subtitle: The architecture that proposed adding guaranteed and predictive real-time service, and link sharing, to best-effort IP.

tldr.problem: Real-time applications such as voice and video often work poorly across the Internet because of variable queueing delays and congestion losses, and IP offers only best-effort delivery.
tldr.mechanism: The memo proposes an integrated services model with guaranteed and predictive real-time service plus controlled link sharing, built from a packet scheduler, a classifier, admission control and the RSVP reservation setup protocol.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational overview that argues the engineering should begin before deployment, and it leaves policy, authentication and several mechanisms for further study.

today: RFC 1633 is an Informational memo from June 1994, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It presents a proposed architecture and argues that the engineering for integrated services must begin before deployment; it leaves policy, authentication and usage feedback for further study.

sections.title: The Problem: Real-Time Traffic on a Best-Effort Network
sections.content:
The multicasts of IETF meetings across the Internet formed a large experiment in sending digitized voice and video through a packet-switched network. The experiments showed that a key element was still missing: real-time applications often do not work well because of variable queueing delays and congestion losses. The Internet, as originally conceived, offers only one quality of service (QoS): point-to-point best-effort delivery.

Network operators want a second thing as well: controlled link-sharing, which divides traffic into a few administrative classes and gives each a minimum percentage of a link's bandwidth under overload, while leaving unused bandwidth available at other times. The memo uses the term integrated services (IS) for a service model that includes best-effort service, real-time service and controlled link-sharing.

The extension must be designed for multicasting from the start, because simply generalizing from the unicast case does not work. The authors believe it is now time to begin the engineering that must precede deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: Live audio and video often arrive too late or damaged because the Internet treats all packets the same. This memo asks for a way to promise some traffic a delivery time, and to share a busy link's bandwidth in a controlled way among groups.

sections.title: Assumptions and the Reference Framework
sections.content:
The proposed extension adds to the Internet architecture rather than replacing it. The key assumption is that resources such as bandwidth must be explicitly managed, so resource reservation and admission control are key building blocks. The memo rejects three arguments against guarantees: that bandwidth will become infinite, that simple priority is enough, and that applications can adapt. It also assumes one common infrastructure and a single internet-layer protocol for real-time and non-real-time traffic, and a single service model for the whole Internet.

This means routers must hold flow-specific state, a change from the principle that flow state lives in end systems. A flow is a distinguishable stream of related datagrams from one user activity that needs the same QoS. A flow is simplex: it has one source and N destinations, so an N-way teleconference generally needs N flows.

The reference implementation framework has four components. The packet scheduler manages forwarding of packet streams using queues at the output driver. The classifier maps each incoming packet into a class that gets the same treatment. Admission control decides whether a new flow can get the requested QoS without harming earlier guarantees. The reservation setup protocol creates and maintains flow-specific state in hosts and routers; the memo's example is RSVP.

An application states its needs with a flowspec, a list of QoS parameters. The setup protocol carries the flowspec, admission control tests it, and the packet scheduler uses it.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers would gain four helpers: a classifier, a scheduler, admission control, and a reservation protocol. Applications describe what they need in a flowspec, and each router accepts or refuses the request.

sections.title: The Integrated Services Model
sections.content:
The core service model deals almost only with the time of delivery, so per-packet delay is the central quantity, and the only quantitative commitments are bounds on maximum and minimum delay. Real-time applications need data by a certain time or the data is worthless; elastic applications always wait for data.

For real-time playback applications, the receiver buffers data and replays it at a fixed offset delay. Intolerant applications need a perfectly reliable delay bound, so the memo proposes guaranteed service. Tolerant and adaptive applications can accept some late packets, so it proposes predictive service: a fairly reliable but not perfectly reliable bound, built on conservative predictions about other flows rather than worst-case assumptions, and presumably cheaper because it allows higher network utilization. Elastic applications get as-soon-as-possible service, called best-effort, in several classes and without admission control.

The model adds link-sharing: share a link's aggregate bandwidth among entities by specified shares, possibly in a hierarchy of organizations, protocols and services. The ideal to approximate is the fluid processor sharing model, where available bandwidth is shared among active entities in proportion to their assigned shares. The memo also proposes preemptable packets a router may discard when service commitments are in danger, and expendable packets so unlikely to be delivered that admission control may ignore them. Usage feedback (accounting) is called a highly contentious issue the memo does not resolve. For reservations, the simplest model is grant-or-refuse; a more complex two-pass model sends offered flowspecs from senders to receivers, then requested flowspecs back, reconciled at each node.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo offers three levels of service: a strict delay guarantee, a softer delay promise that costs less, and normal best-effort delivery. It also lets an operator divide a link's bandwidth among groups, with the shares applying only under overload.

sections.title: Traffic Control Mechanisms
sections.content:
In the forwarding path a router can select a route, then forward, drop, reorder or hold a packet. Packet scheduling reorders the output queue. Strict priority gives some packets absolute preference, and enough high-priority traffic can stop the lower class entirely. Round-robin variants such as Weighted Fair Queueing (WFQ) instead allocate a link's bandwidth into specified shares.

Packet dropping matters as much as scheduling. For TCP over best-effort IP, a drop is a signal of congestion and causes the sender to reduce its load. For real-time traffic, dropping one packet from a queue reduces the delay of every packet behind it. Simple schemes such as a single global buffer pool can defeat a WFQ service objective, so dropping and scheduling must be coordinated.

Classification needs more than the destination address: the classifier may look at the source address, protocol number and port fields, or a cached "flow-id" field might shortcut the work. Admission control may compute from worst-case service parameters or from measured usage; the algorithm in each router is a local matter, so vendors can compete on it.

A theoretical result by Parekh shows that if a router implements WFQ and the traffic source is characterized, for example by a token bucket bound, there is an absolute upper bound on network delay, and it is the best possible under those assumptions. As a proof of concept the memo describes the CSZ scheme: WFQ isolates guaranteed flows, priority separates predictive from best-effort service, FIFO mixes traffic inside each predictive sub-class, and WFQ provides link sharing inside best-effort. The memo stresses that CSZ is not mandatory; for links known to be underloaded, FIFO delivers satisfactory service.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can line packets up by strict priority or by fair shares; the memo prefers fair shares, because priority can starve other traffic. Dropping a packet also helps: it signals congestion to TCP and cuts delay for real-time queues.

sections.title: RSVP: Receiver-Initiated Soft State
sections.content:
A reservation setup protocol must be designed for multicast, accommodate heterogeneous receivers, scale to large groups, and support advance reservation. RSVP was designed to meet these requirements. A session is defined by the common IP multicast destination address of the receivers. A reservation request pairs a flowspec (the amount of resources) with a filter spec (which packets receive them); the flowspec parametrizes the packet scheduler and the filter spec is installed in the classifier.

RSVP offers three reservation styles. A wildcard reservation uses a filter spec that is not source-specific, so all packets of the session share one pool, useful for an audio conference where few sources are active at once. Fixed-filter reservations select particular sources and cannot change during their lifetime without re-invoking admission control. Dynamic-filter reservations let a receiver change its source choice over time without additional admission control, at the cost of allocating for the worst case.

Reservations are receiver-initiated: each receiver learns the senders' offered flowspecs by a higher-level mechanism, generates its own desired flowspec, and propagates it toward the senders, installing reservations in each router along the way. Receiver initiation handles heterogeneous receivers and matches IP multicast, where receivers join a group. RSVP uses soft state: reservation state is cached information installed and periodically refreshed by the end hosts, and unused state is timed out by the routers. If a route changes, the refresh messages automatically install state along the new route.

The memo lists four routing issues: finding a route that supports reservation, finding one with enough capacity, adapting to a route failure, and adapting to a route change without failure, for which it suggests "route pinning". RSVP is designed to work with any current routing protocol without modification, which the memo calls a short-term compromise.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver, not the sender, asks for the reservation, which scales to large multicast groups. Each router keeps that request only as soft state: hosts refresh it periodically, and routers drop it when refreshes stop.

sections.title: Authentication and Policy
sections.content: Resource reservation means some users get privileged service, so policy and administrative controls will be needed. That leads to two authentication requirements: authentication of the users who make reservation requests, and authentication of the packets that claim the right to use reserved resources. The memo notes these issues are not unique to integrated services; commercialization and commercial security lead to the same requirements. It does not discuss policy or security further and leaves the issues for study.
sections.plainLanguage: Reserved service is privileged service, so the network must check who may reserve and which packets may use the reservation. The memo leaves both questions for further study.
